utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we call the witness, maybe just one little point to look at. There was an application, if I can find my glasses, by the Prosecution, on the 25th of January 2006, to admit certain statements in terms of Rule 92 bis. You will recall that the statement of M-28 was sent back for the Prosecution to make certain corrections on it. The Chamber is now ready to make the order in relation to the original motion and the subsequent motion. I'm going to read the order. It's an oral order. The Trial Chamber will now render its decision on both the Prosecution's motion for the admission of the statement of Witness MM-028 of the 25th of January 2006, and its subsequent motion for the admission of additional statement of MM-028 pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the 30th of March 2006. 2: The Trial Chamber considers that the Prosecution has complied with the Trial Chamber's oral ruling of the 15th of January -- I beg your pardon, 15th of February 2006 and that the Prosecution has demonstrated sufficient reliability of the documents associated with the original statement of Witness MM-028. The original statement of Witness MM-028 and the documents associated therewith are admitted into evidence. 3: The Prosecution also seeks the admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis of an additional statement of witness MM-028 including attached documents. The Trial Chamber recalls its decision of the 16th of January 2006 wherein it set out the applicable law pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Trial Chamber considers that the additional statement does not go to the acts or conduct of the accused, that the original of the documents is identified by the witness in the additional statement and that the documents refer to events relevant to this case. The Prosecution's motion is granted and the additional statement and the attached documents are admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. 4: The Trial Chamber requests the Registrar to assign exhibit numbers to the two statements of Witness MM-028 and the documents attached to them. Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I might first take the occasion briefly of Your Honour's return to express the Prosecution's deepest condolences for Your Honour's loss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are deeply sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To pass from the profound to the banal, if I might deal with one other housekeeping matter which is Exhibit number 241, if Your Honours will recall, this is an exhibit that came up, was offered by the Defence, was going to be used by the Defence during the cross-examination of Witness Milan Babic, as I recall. In any event it was an exhibit for which there was no translation into English. And the Court asked if the Prosecution would undertake having that document translated. The document has been translated. The translation is now available in e-court. The exhibit was marked for identification. I believe it's the only remaining -- it may be the only remaining document that's marked for identification at this point. I don't know if the Defence seeks its admission into evidence but if it does, the Prosecution would have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. First of all, I wish to take this opportunity, Your Honour, on the occasion of the tragedy that has befallen you and your family to express the deepest condolences of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to this document, we tender it into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Then the document will be admitted into evidence. And may it please be given an exhibit number that was given Exhibit number 241 for identification. I guess it will retain the number 241.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit number 241, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Black will be handling the next witness so I now defer to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution will now call our next witness, Mr. Rade Raseta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. Can you understand me in your own language?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If at any time you have difficulty understanding one of my questions, please just tell me and I'll try to state it more clearly. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, I'll begin with a few questions about your personal and professional background. First, could you please state your name for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: My name is Rade Raseta, and I'm a retired colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you born in Donji Lapac, Croatia, in 1947?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And although you were born in Croatia, you were ethnically Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you please briefly describe your education and your professional posts up until the year 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: After completing primary school in the place of my birth, I continued my education in the school for non-commissioned officers for armoured units of the JNA and I graduated from there in 1964. After I completed the secondary military school, I was sent to serve in Skopje in the Republic of Macedonia. From 1964 until 1975, I performed all troop command duties at a lower level, commandeer duties, and in 1977 I passed an exam to become an officer and I was promoted to commissioned officer status as second lieutenant. In 1975, I was accepted in the security service of the JNA, and in that same year, I was sent for training and education. In 1976, I completed the training course for security. In the security services I performed the following duties: I was chief of the security organ in the command at brigade and regiment level. I was an officer in the division, at the division level, for security. Then I was an officer in the counterintelligence group of the army command. I was the chief of the information analysis department in the army command, chief of the information analysis department in the security department of the Main Staff of the Serb Army of Krajina, chief of the security department of the Main Staff of the Serb Army of the Krajina. In the Republic of Serbian Krajina, I served from October 1993 until the second half of August 1995. After the fall of the Krajina, at my own request, and because I fulfilled the conditions for retirement, one of the conditions, on the 1st of January 1996, I retired. That is it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, colonel. Just a couple of questions about what you've just told us. Where did you serve between, let's say, 1975 and 1992? In what location?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Throughout this time, I was in the Republic of Macedonia, in the Kumanovo garrison and in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you change location in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After the break-up of the SFRY, the command of the army was relocated from Skopje to the Nis garrison. I was there from 1992 until I left for the Krajina in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, colonel. Now, I'll ask you some questions about how you came to serve in the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, known as the SVK. First of all, did you volunteer to serve in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: To the SVK, I went under orders from the chief of the General Staff of the army of the FRY, General Perisic. He sent me there to serve on a temporary basis for up to one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so I understand, did you volunteer for that position or you were simply assigned?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No, I did not volunteer. I was assigned. I was issued an order from the chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And another question to make sure it's clear, did you leave the Yugoslav army, the VJ, in order to serve in the SVK or did you remain in the service of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I retained the status of an officer of the VJ with all the entitlements. For example, my family received my salary on my personal account and in the Republic of Serb Krajina we had certain privileges. For example, we were paid 15 per cent on our salary as a kind of hardship allowance, and also our time of service there was counted double for pension purposes. Those were the benefits we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who was it who paid your salary? Was it the Yugoslav army or the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It was the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of how many VJ officers, including yourself, were serving in command positions in the SVK while you were there in 1993, 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I can't tell you the precise number but approximately it was between 150 and 200 officers in leading positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were these officers originally from the territory of the RSK or not necessarily, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: For the most part, an effort was made to have them from the RSK, originally from there, or to have people who were born in the Republic of Croatia. Someone might have been born in the Republic of Croatia but not in the RSK. However, if he was an ethnic Serb, he could have been assigned to work on a temporary basis in the Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That leads to my next question. What was the ethnic makeup of this group of VJ officers serving in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: For the most part, the officers who were sent like me to work there on a temporary basis were ethnic Serbs. There were, however, a few officers, a small number of other ethnicities. I know about one Muslim, one Macedonian and so on, who happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if these other officers, other than yourself, did they volunteer to serve in the SVK or were they simply assigned, as you were?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: According to my personal estimate, there were 20 or 30 per cent of these officers who volunteered. All the others were sent there under orders from the General Staff, like myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And finally on this topic, was there a standard duration for service in the SVK, a standard amount of time that you were sent there for?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This was a time period of up to one year. Following the expiry of which, everyone was entitled to return to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. However, under the proviso that one applied for it in writing and then some of these applications would be granted, others were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You yourself served in the SVK for more than one year. How did that happen in your case?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It happened the following way. After the expiry of my service there, the department itself, the service, requested that I remain and my commander, General Celeketic, insisted that I stay for a further period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, now I'm going to change topic slightly and I'll ask you some questions about your duties in the SVK security organs. First, you briefly covered this when you told us about your professional positions but please remind me which positions you held during the time you were in the SVK.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: On my arrival in Krajina, for one year I was chief of the information analysis department of the security administration of the Main Staff. This was the period up to December 1994. When my immediate superior chief went to Belgrade, the commander of the Main Staff ordered that I become chief of security of the Main Staff and I accepted that duty on the 19th of December 1994 and I continued performing the duty until such time as I left Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Can you describe generally the tasks of the SVK security services while you were there, while you served there?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: For the most part, the duties stemmed from the duties held by the security service of the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. First of all, the service performed the duties aimed at monitoring and intercepting the activities of the other foreign services and the adequate services in the SVK were informed accordingly. Secondly, the preventive activities, prevention of internal destructive forces in the SVK forces aimed at undermining the morale and the combat readiness of the units. Crime prevention, for the most part dealing with the crime against the commands and units of the army, namely theft of combat hardware, explosives and other type of weaponry. We also took part in drafting regulations and rules of security, preventive measures, which were sent on to the commands of units. We also administered units of the military police, and lastly we organised and carried out cooperation with UNPROFOR and other international institutions and organisations stationed in Krajina, but only so far as the personal and collective security and safety was threatened as far as there were attempts to misappropriate army resources and so on. Generally speaking, these were the duties that the service dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what were your own duties with relation to those tasks, first as the head of the information analysis section and subsequently as head of the entire security services of the SVK Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: As the head of the information analysis, I received all the information, whereupon I analysed and examined the information, drafted documents and proposed measures to the chief aimed at improving and ensuring the execution of the duties that I have just mentioned. When I assumed the duty of the chief of security, I managed the entire service and dealt with intelligence -- the security issues in the SVK but not only in the Main Staff. I also worked with the lower-ranking security services directly involved in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, you mentioned crime prevention. Did your duties or the tasks of the security organs also include the investigation of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: To my knowledge, for the duration of my stay there, there was a team dealing with war crimes. I know that Savo Strbac headed the team and out of the security department, Colonel Suput was involved in these activities. Periodically, I was informed by my subordinates on the results of their work, and as far as I remember, war crimes committed against Serbs by Croat forces were being investigated. I don't remember the specific cases at hand, but I do know that this was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember any cases of war crimes committed by Serb forces against Croat forces being investigated or reported?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: For as long as I was there in Krajina, this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And why do you think that was? Why do you think there were no reports of such crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't know. My personal opinion is that there was no wish to do so. Based on what I learnt previously, there must have been such crimes and there must have been space there for these crimes to be investigated. Why this was not done, I cannot say, but I am certain that there were instruments in place to investigate crimes on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, from whom did you receive your orders when you were head of the SVK security organs?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I received orders solely from the commander of the Main Staff, General Celeketic and later on General Mrksic. However, from time to time I received tasks from the then president, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: About how many times did you have direct interaction with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I had about ten contacts with President Martic. Some of these were on my initiative and some on the initiative of the then president.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what tasks or topics were discussed on those occasions, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The advancement of the security service of Krajina was discussed, namely the ways of unifying the service. Regardless of who headed the service, there was time -- this was the time for the service to be brought under one chapeau, as it were. Furthermore, there were criminal activities taking place. For instance, fuel tankers arriving from the Republic of Serbia were being misappropriated, on their way from Republika Srpska to the RSK. I remember well that once 16 fuel tankers and trucks with barrels entered the country and president Martic ordered that we -- that I establish the department of the military police and receive the convoy at Raca border crossing. I did as I was ordered. However, the column was intercepted by some armed, unidentified persons who disarmed my military policemen, and these tankers went somewhere, nobody knows where. Only three of these 16 tankers actually reached the Main Staff of the RSK. This was one such assignment. I remember another such assignment when Captain Dragan Vasiljkovic - I don't know where this took place, I can't remember - stole some boat engines and then put them on a trailer-truck. There were some other equipment there too but the engines were easy to be seen because they were new and they were moth-balled, and he tried to take them to the Republic of Serbia. However, I informed General Celeketic thereof. He in turn informed Mr. Martic, and our president intervened through Milosevic. Milosevic said that the convoy should be allowed to proceed towards Serbia and that his men were to wait for the convoy there. I also interacted with him when I was supposed to secure the presidential palace where he worked. It was my guard that had to deal with the security issues, and that was the one occasion when I had contacts with him. There were other such contacts but I can't remember them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, colonel. Did Mr. Martic ever say anything to you about his attitude towards Croats in general?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He did. On one occasion, I can't remember what this contact was about, I remember him telling me that he could not be a nationalist, he could not make himself hate Croats. He even told me that once he completed the MUP school, his first service entailed him staying at the home of Croats with whom he continued being in touch, even at that date. He told me whoever was saying that I was a nationalist and hated Croats was wrong. And I believed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were Martic's actions in 1994-1995 consistent with what he'd told you, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't know which actions you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just in general. Any actions. Did you feel like Mr. Martic acted in accordance with what he told you, as you just explained to us?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period of 1994 and 1995 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the entire time you were there.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, one could not put it that way, in view of the measures taken against the Croat side. For instance, the shelling of Zagreb, then the order to fire upon Sisak and some other towns, in the wake of Operation Flash. Perhaps there were other such attacks. This went to directly contradict Mr. Martic's statement concerning his attitude towards Croats, if I've understood your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, I think you understood my question. Let me change topics slightly and ask you if there was any formal or informal collaboration between the SVK security organs and the RSK minister -- Ministry of the Interior while were you chief of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That cooperation was pretty weak. We were in touch. However, the tasks we agreed upon were never really carried out. In other words, there were contacts but there was no cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go very briefly into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, now let me ask you about a different topic, about the relations between the SVK and the Yugoslav army during the time that you served in the Krajina. You've already told us about the provision of Yugoslav army personnel, such as yourself, to the SVK. Did the VJ also provide logistical support to the SVK, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The army of the Republic of Serb Krajina and the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were actually one and the same organisation, but positioned at two different locations. Now, why do I say this? In addition to the personnel that was assigned to the Republic of Serbian Krajina at all levels, all the possible logistical support was provided too, starting from fuel, ammunition, weaponry, foodstuffs, quartermasters' supplies, professional support in planning and executing actions, as well as a number of other kinds of support.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you some specific questions on this topic then, about other kinds of support. Was there any similarity in the procedures and methods applied by the SVK security organs and the security services of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. As a whole our activities were based on the rules and instructions issued by the security administration of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We therefore had the same rules and regulations, the same operations methods, and procedures. There was no difference whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: While you were serving in the SVK security organs, did you report to anyone in the Yugoslav army about your activities?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely because of what I've just told you, that we used all the instructions, rules and operations and technical resources and personnel from the security administration of the FRY, we were duty-bound to inform the security administration of all our activities. This was something that I myself had to do, just as all my predecessors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And whom in the VJ did you inform specifically?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Inform or report to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all, you've heard Judge Moloto's question. Was this reporting or informing? Was there a difference there?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, there is. We only submitted reports, or rather we reported on our activities. We were not able to be held answerable for any omissions on our part. I could be punished by Dimitrijevic and General Celeketic, to make this clear. Or rather I could not be punished by Dimitrijevic but by Celeketic only, so therefore we only informed them. But this was the case precisely because we used the rules and instructions and the methods of work employed by the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was for this reason that we were duty-bound to inform them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you mentioned a General Dimitrijevic, as well as a General Celeketic. Who were those two men, just so we are clear?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic, Aleksandar Dimitrijevic was the chief of the security administration of the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and General Celeketic was the Commander of the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In your testimony, I believe is that you informed General Dimitrijevic but you didn't report to him in the sense that you were not answerable to him but you were answerable to General Celeketic of the SVK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Does that clear it up, Your Honour, or should I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have to understand that it's your evidence that there was nobody in the Yugoslav army to whom you reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How, then, do you explain vis-a-vis yourself, the relationship between the VJ and the SVK? You said they are one and the same thing, and you said that logistical support came from the VJ to the SVK. Now, it does seem as if you had no responsibility whatsoever to the VJ but only to the SVK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was responsible in terms of having to inform them of the way in which the resources were applied and which activities were undertaken. All the information flowed to this one location, and that was the security administration, but I repeat, General Dimitrijevic was not able to apply any sanctions against me. It was only General Celeketic who could do that. However, I still had the obligation to inform him, to report on the activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The information that you passed on to General Dimitrijevic, were you duty-bound to do so or were you just informing him? I hear you talk of inform instead of report. And what I do want to understand is did you just inform him because you wanted to inform him or did you inform him because you were duty-bound to inform him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was duty-bound to inform him whenever we applied measures or used the military hardware and personnel, and I'm referring to special hardware. I had to inform him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, and maybe you've alluded to this somewhat, but what kinds of information did you forward, let's say, to General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't understand, what kind of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What kind of information -- you've told us how you were duty bound to inform General Dimitrijevic about certain activities or certain issues and I'd like you to tell us what activities or issues those were. Just generally.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It had to do with the activities where methods of work and resources were used. I believe that this does come under the confidentiality issue. I believe that there are certain issues I should not touch upon. But these were some very specific measures and persons that were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think that's sufficient for our purposes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just interrupt. To what extent does the confidentiality go? In other words, do I understand the witness to be saying if we went into private session he would disclose or would the -- the confidentiality prohibits him from even mentioning those in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. Perhaps the witness can give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope my answer will be clear. There was a certain number of officers who were being dealt with by the security service in the army of Yugoslavia. These were transferred to the SVK. However, the operative surveillance of these officers continued and they were the ones I was duty-bound to report about to the FRY. I don't recall the names of the officers now but the continuity of surveillance had to be maintained regardless of where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have the impression that the information that you passed to the Yugoslavia Slav army and in particular to General Dimitrijevic, was that information received and used? Did you have any impression about that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. I did have an impression, in particular the specific cases we've just been mentioning but also all other information of significance to the armed forces, whatever the topic of my reports. Sometimes I was told what further information I had to obtain, and, yes, this information was used in the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Based on your interaction with General Dimitrijevic and maybe others in the VJ, did you form an opinion or an impression of the VJ's position towards Mr. Martic, whether they supported or opposed Mr. Martic or had no position whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He received their full support.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you explain a little bit what leads you to say that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I say that because on one occasion, General Dimitrijevic personally told me, when I was reporting to him in his office, that we should do everything to support President Martic, that he was on the right track, and that he was doing everything in his power for the Serbs in the Republic of Serbian Krajina to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about Milan Babic? Did you have an impression of the VJ's position towards Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Milan Babic did not enjoy any authority or respect with the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And do you have any opinion about where this differing policy towards Mr. Martic and Mr. Babic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question because we had a microphone problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, do you have any opinion about where this policy originated, the support of Martic and the lack of support for Babic? Did you have an impression at the time as to who was driving this policy?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The policy supporting Mr. Martic was driven by Mr. Milosevic, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, of course. However, the policy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not to support Mr. Babic. That's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if your superiors in the SVK, in particular General Celeketic, or Mr. Martic, knew that you were informing the VJ about your activities?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I reported to General Celeketic from time to time, as needed. But I did not report to President Martic because he was not my immediate superior at the time. If need be, it was General Celeketic who informed Mr. Martic. I was not duty-bound to report to Mr. Martic directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You've described now for us the way in which you cooperated with your, let's say your counterparts in the VJ. Do you know if other officers in the SVK Main Staff also cooperated with their counterparts on the VJ General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I know that occasionally the assistant commander for logistics, for example, or the assistant commander for morale, or for organisation and mobilisation, or the chief of the intelligence department, would occasionally go to the FRY General Staff for consultations, exchange of information, and so on, and I don't know whether I've answered all of your question. There was, however, communication between the chiefs of these various sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to show you a document. It will appear on the screen in front of you in just a moment. The 65 ter number is 1878, if the Court officer can please bring that up on e-court. Are you able to see the document on your screen there, Colonel? Colonel, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This document was compiled in the Main Staff of the Serb Army of the Krajina, and it refers to the daily reporting. It's an order from the Main Staff of the Serb Army of Krajina, saying that combat reports were to be sent to the General staff of the army of Yugoslavia and that they were to contain the information listed below.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could look at the second page briefly, please, it's the second in both B/C/S and English, colonel, can you see who signed this order?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This order was signed by the then commander of the Main Staff, Brigadier General Mile Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if this order was in fact implemented?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This order was drawn up at about the time when I arrived in the Krajina, but at that time, I was not able to contact the commander of the Main Staff and his assistants in view of the nature of my work. But when I was chief of the security organ of the Main Staff, this kind of reporting continued. These issues listed here were those on which regular reports were sent to the Main Staff, army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What if anything does this tell us about the relationship between the SVK Main Staff and the General Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, this shows that there was almost a relationship of subordination of the SVK Main Staff towards the General staff of the army of Yugoslavia. They had the obligation imposed upon them to send combat reports. The Main Staff of Yugoslavia imposed the obligation on the General Staff of the SVK to send them these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would offer this document into evidence and ask that it be assigned an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 456, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one very, very short topic before we take the next break. Colonel, do you know -- this is a slight change of topic, but do you know if there was any formalised exchange of information between the SVK security organs and the security organs of the Bosnian Serb army, the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the time before I became chief of the security organ of the Main Staff. However, from that time, I attempted to establish cooperation with the then general, Zdravko Tolimir, but I was not successful in this. He was not in favour of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to start another topic. Perhaps it would be a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's a convenient time for the break. Shall we take a break and come back at 4.00? Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, we've been discussing cooperation and I'm going to move to a new topic in just a moment but there are actually one or two questions I'd like to ask you before we change topics. We've been speaking mostly about the military but do you know if members of the police of the Republic of Serbia served in the RSK police in the same general way that you, as a member of the VJ, served in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I did not observe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And as the head of the SVK security organs, did you cooperate with any officials from the police of the Republic of Serbia on the territory of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: When Mrksic was appointed commander of the Main Staff on the 18th of May 1995, he introduced me to the state security organ from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whose name was Milan Knezevic, who had arrived to unify all the security services in the Krajina. He's the only organ I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you say that Mr. Knezevic belonged apparently to the state security organ of the FRY. Could you just explain to me whether that's a military or police position?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That is a civilian post, or a police post. It doesn't belong to the military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Colonel Raseta, now I'm going to turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just clarify one thing? I'm going to ask you the same question but in relation to a different police force. Did you, in your capacity as a chief in the SAO Krajina, cooperate with the police of the SAO Krajina at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. We did have contacts, but not cooperation. Not the kind of cooperation envisioned in our former instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What kind of contact did you have with the SAO Krajina Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had contacts with the representatives of the MUP and the State Security in order to further mutual cooperation. This is what President Martic insisted on at the time. However, we would get together and agree on joint tasks and then nothing would happen. It would all fail to materialise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But do I understand you to be saying that you had this contact to agree on joint tasks at the insistence of Mr. Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before we move on, I just want to get it on the record, the witness has referred to the state security organ and he has spoken of a Milan Knezevic. What office did this person hold? Because I see a reference to chief security organ which would tend to refer to a body. What was his actual office? You have told us what his duties were, what he was attempting to do but can I hear what office he held, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know his precise office, but he was introduced to me as a representative of the State Security Service of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who had been sent to the Krajina, I assume by Jovica Stanisic, to coordinate and unify the work of all State Security Services and the Military Security Services of the territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, now I'm going to ask you to turn to another topic and that's command and control within the SVK. First of all, can you explain what the RSK Supreme Defence Council was?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The RSK Supreme Defence Council was the highest body commanding the armed forces in the republic. It consisted of the president, Mr. Milan Martic, who was also the Commander-in-Chief, then General Celeketic, who was the commander of the Main Staff, the Minister of Defence, the Prime Minister, the speaker of parliament when needed, the Minister of the Interior. These people were the members of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You may have mentioned this in your previous answer, but who was the Supreme Commander of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The Supreme Commander was Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was Mr. Martic the de jure Supreme Commander or the de facto Supreme Commander of the SVK or both?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Both de jure and de facto, both.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you explain a little bit your basis for saying that he was the de facto commander of the SVK? Supreme Commander, I mean.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, this was provided for by the constitution. That's the first thing. And secondly, at the proposal of the Commander of the Main Staff on the use of the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, a decision would be made and issued by the President of the republic. All operative work was done by the Main Staff, but it was the president of the republic who gave his blessing, and who also issued the decision on the use of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What was Mr. Martic's role in the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: To command the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is there anything more specific that he did in the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask it in a different way. Who presided over the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The president of the republic, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How would you characterise Mr. Martic's knowledge of military matters, or his understanding of military matters?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The president of the republic, Milan Martic, did not know -- he did not have the same knowledge about the use of the armed forces that professional soldiers have, but that's why he had the chief of the Main Staff and other military men who made proposals to President Martic about the use of the armed forces. It was up to him to hear them out and then to either agree or disagree with the decision they proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You made reference to the chief of the Main Staff and other military men. Was there anyone in particular who Milan Martic relied upon for advice on military matters?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff, General Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know when General Celeketic became the Commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I'm not sure but I think it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed him to that position?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The president of the republic, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How would you describe the relationship between Martic and Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The appointment of General Celeketic shows that Mr. Milan Martic had the most confidence in him of all the others in the Krajina, all the other officers, which is why he appointed him. In Martic's estimation, he was the most able officer and therefore he appointed him to command the Main Staff. Nobody told me this, but that's how things worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Separate from the actual appointment of General Celeketic, were there any other indications of this relationship between the two men that you personally observed?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: One could observe that the two of them had been on close terms, even before, that they were good pals and that their friendship dated from before. I don't know from where, when, exactly, but they respected each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did General Celeketic consult with Martic on military matters or did he take decisions independently at any time?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: As far as I was able to observe, he was in contact with Milan Martic. However, he always tried to first take a decision with his own staff and then inform Mr. Martic about the decision taken and the proposed measures and the ways of carrying them out, which would be efficient. As far as the armed forces of the RSK were concerned, he always prepared everything beforehand and then put forth his proposals to Milan Martic, who would then accept such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did General Celeketic ever take a decision and implement a decision without the approval of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I am not aware of anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, now I'm going to ask you about Martic's relations with several other senior figures in the FRY and the RSK and elsewhere, in fact. We've already discussed a little bit General Celeketic. So now I'll ask you about Slobodan Milosevic. First of all, what position did Mr. Milosevic hold at this time, while you were serving in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He was the president of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- no, the president of the Republic of Serbia, and then at a later date the president of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I believe, unless I'm mistaken. I know for a fact that he was president of the Republic of Serbia. I cannot say exactly when it was that he was elected president of the FRY. There was Zoran Ilic, who was his predecessor there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Zoran Lilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he was definitely the president of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The more important question is how would you describe the relationship between these two men, Milan Martic and Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic wielded his full influence over Milan Martic. He respected Milan Martic and did everything in his power to ensure that Milan Martic remained president of the RSK. All his efforts were directed at fulfilling this goal to the full.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you give any specific examples of this support or this influence?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The most overriding example is the logistical support provided to the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Secondly, this is something that General Dimitrijevic told me personally, that it was Milosevic's position that we should do everything in our power to make sure that Milan Martic remained head of state, that this was the guarantee for the survival of the Serbs in Krajina and of the existence of the link with the mother country. That was the prevalent feeling among the top military leadership, that this was the sort of attitude and sentiments that Mr. Milosevic had vis-a-vis Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Milosevic had any influence on Mr. Martic's position towards the Z-4 peace plan?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that on that day when a team from the Krajina led by President Martic set out to discuss the Z-4 plan, I believe that they used an UNPROFOR helicopter for that purpose. Although I don't know the -- what the contents of the plan were precisely, I know that the helicopter flew out holding our representatives for these negotiations and I believe that Mr. Akashi chaired the meeting. Before the helicopter took off from Knin, the chief of office of Mr. Martic, I believe his name was Knezevic, reached the Heliodrom and told him that Mr. Milosevic had said that the plan, the Z-4 plan, be a priori rejected without any prior discussion. I heard this from Mihajlo Knezevic who told me that the main boss in Belgrade had said that the Z-4 plan be rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic exercise his influence over Martic directly or personally or indirectly or both -- in both ways?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I meant both ways. One was the direct communication with Mr. Martic, and the second was whenever Jovica Stanisic came over, he relayed any instructions he had from Mr. Milosevic to Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know how often Mr. Martic had direct communication with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not privy to such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if he ever had direct communication with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hasn't that question been answered already? I thought the witness said he had both direct and indirect influence over Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. Thank you. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, now I'd like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 1470 and I'd ask the assistance of the Court officer to bring that up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, if you could just look at the first page of this document and tell us what this is if you can tell.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This is a regular operations report compiled at the Main Staff of the Serb Army of Krajina and was delivered to the Office of the President of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic, to the office of the president of the Serbian Krajina, Mr. Milan Martic, and the chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army personally to Colonel General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: According to JNA and VJ doctrine, was it normal for a regular combat report to be sent to the president of another republic, in this case the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Which persons ordinarily receive regular combat reports?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: A report such as this one was supposed to be sent first to the office of President Martic and second, in view of the obligation we have mentioned earlier, that there was the order to submit written reports to the General Staff of the Yugoslav army, it was quite logical that a report where it was intended to be sent to the Army of Yugoslavia, it should have been addressed to the chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army, Colonel General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question is actually -- it's a little bit more general than that and if you don't understand it let me know and I'll try to ask it in a different way. Which kinds of persons ordinarily receive regular combat reports? Are these widely distributed or are there certain kinds of people who ordinarily receive them?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This particular report was supposed to be sent to General Momcilo Perisic, and that's based on the obligations the SVK had, in terms of writing reports to the General Staff of the Yugoslav army. Therefore it was Perisic who was supposed to receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understand that. My question is more general, not just with regard to this document but with all regular combat reports, would those be delivered widely or through the chain of command or to a particular person? What kinds of people ordinarily receive such reports under standard military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Under the customary military doctrine, one had to follow the chain of command. President Milosevic was not a person who was supposed to receive such reports; on no account, if I understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And can any conclusion be drawn from the fact that Mr. Milosevic personally was an addressee of this report?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The conclusion takes us back to what I touched upon earlier, and that's the influence that Milosevic wanted to have, not only over the political events but also over the army of the RSK. I can't see that there is anything else. He tried to make sure to have influence over all the infrastructure in the RSK, including the army of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please, and be assigned an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 457, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, now I'm going to turn to another person. Someone you've mentioned already in your testimony. Who was Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic was the chief of the State Security of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did he have in the affairs of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He had a command at Petrova Gora, where a certain number of members of the Serbian MUP were located, and he visited them on several occasions, and very often he appeared in the RSK as a special envoy of the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic. It was in this capacity that he toured the Krajina, visiting the special units at Petrova Gora. I know that on one occasion, for a fact, he contacted Mr. Martic, and the commander of the Main Staff when he was at the forward command post at Titova Korenica. He was a person who was respected everywhere in Serbia and even beyond, including the Krajina, because of his close relations with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how would you describe his relationship with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't know what their relationship was but I know that Jovica Stanisic contacted Milan Martic. Now, whether Martic respected him or not, I don't know. At any rate, he implemented whatever Stanisic told him had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you about someone else now. Who was Dragan Vasiljkovic? You've also referred to him earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: When I arrived in the Krajina, Dragan Vasiljkovic was commander of the Alpha Centre in Bruska. It was a centre for the training of Special Forces. However, Dragan was involved in some dishonourable business as well. I already said that he misappropriated property such as boat engines and some other items I can't recall at present. We had circumstantial evidence but because we didn't have enough time, we did not investigate into that. There were allegations of him dismantling some UNPROFOR vehicles and then transporting them over to the Republic of Serbia. This was the person and this is my assumption who was installed there by the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia for their own purposes, that he executed over there. He was carrying around a topographical map and he said that he had carried out some 137 operations aimed at the Republic of Serbia which consisted of reconnaissance of different towns.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, operations aimed at the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not carry out any sort of training, at least not for the operations he professed to do. He had a squad or a platoon of young girls who for the most part were of dubious moral integrity or simply had no where else to go but to be accepted down there. Most of the soldiers he trained down there were deserters from our units, from the army of the RSK, after whom we sent out searches because of desertion and they were in hiding among his units, and that's the way things stood until we sent over our own security official at the centre who was a subordinate of Captain Dragan's, but had to report and be answerable to our security body and it was through him that we obtained most of the information which had to do with the misconduct of Captain Dragan's. He ruined one helicopter, and I believe that as a result of this the pilot involved was permanently disabled. He took part in some very significant meetings at the command of the Main Staff. When I assumed my duty, I reported to General Celeketic and told him that we could not discuss our matters in the same office where Captain Dragan was and from that point on, he never appeared again. I know that he would drop by president Martic's office. I know that he went every where in an attempt to secure his stay there as long as he could. I believe that prior to the fall of Krajina, he left the area. I'm not sure about that, but I never saw him there again. And that's the story concerning him in the briefest of terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How would you describe his relationship with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The same way I did for all the others. In view of the fact that the MUP of Serbia or the state security department appointed him down there, we had to respect him on that account. I know that this went for Mr. Martic as well. I don't know whether he respected him indeed but he did receive him in his office. I don't know what opinion he held in his regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about another person. What was the relationship between Milan Martic and Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The two of them could not get along at all. This sort of situation existed even before I arrived there. As for the reasons underlying their disagreement, I am not aware of them. But I know that the Republic of Serbia did not accept Mr. Babic. I know that they supported Mr. Martic, and that's the long and the short of what I know of him. Regardless of the fact that he was in the executive government. I believe that he was the foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did Mr. Babic run for president against Mr. Martic in 1994, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He did. I remember that quite well. The elections were won by the late Milan Babic. However, I suppose this was a reaction from the Republic of Serbia, where they asked for the annulment of the elections and for a new round of elections to make sure that Milan Martic won them. In connection with this, there were some ballot boxes that were being disposed of. One such box was found in the park next to the command of the Main Staff. We found them and we handed them over to the MUP. I apologise. The elections were found to have been irregular and rigged, and the second round of elections was won by Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, just to let you know, there is some water next to you so if you need to take a drink of water, feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just get the point. The elections that were won by Mr. Martic, are these the ones that were rigged?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, if you understand the question, please go ahead and answer.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, who was Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic was the president of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How would you describe his relationship, if any, with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Based on what could be heard from the mass media and from conversations with the officers, I knew that they were on good terms. I remember a visit by President Karadzic to the RSK when he was received with all state honours by President Martic and this was at the fortress. The story went at the time and still goes around today that the relationship between the two was such that President Martic called -- addressed him as "scholar" and Karadzic addressed Martic as "warrior." I wasn't involved in the visit except for counterintelligence activities but I heard from my chief that the objective of the visit was to make a preliminary -- to make preliminary agreements about -- or for the unification of the RSK and the Republika Srpska. There was discussion of a referendum following which the two republics were supposed to be unified. Several days later, a reaction followed from Mr. Milosevic to the effect that no referendum should be held at all and that the situation should remain as it was at the time. And that's as much as I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, colonel. Now I'm going to move to yet another topic and I'd like to focus your attention on May of 1995. And I'd like you to look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is trial Exhibit 93, if it could be brought up on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you'll just be patient, Colonel. We are having a bit of a technical problem. In a moment we'll blow it up so you can look at it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is it possible to zoom in a bit on the document or is it not working?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, do you see the document on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, if we could scroll just up a little bit so the heading of the document is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What's the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The 26th of May 1995. That's when it was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we please look at the last page of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, does your signature appear here on the last page?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you draft this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This document was created by the intelligence officer in the intelligence department. I copied this and used it for my own needs in order to check certain information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could again look at the first page, please, if we could scroll down to about the second paragraph there that kind of has a bracket around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, what is being referred to here on the first page of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: General Celeketic ordered the commander of the 39th Corps to open artillery fire on Sisak out of retaliation against the Croatian forces who had committed aggression on Western Slavonia. The commander of the 39th corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. It's not necessary to read it out. I think you've explained now generally what it was about. Who was present on this occasion when General Celeketic ordered artillery fire on Sisak?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: All the assistants of General Celeketic were there, General Bjelanovic, General Loncar, myself, Colonel Mihajlo Knezevic, the assistant for morale and moral guidance, and for operations and training, Colonel Milisav Sekulic. In the meantime, before the command was issued, before the order was issued to the commander of the 39th corps to fire on Sisak, President Martic came into General Celeketic's office. He heard General Celeketic's decision and after the order was issued to Gacic to fire on Sisak, President Martic left the office. That's what I know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On what date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarity here? Some of the names, Mr. Raseta, that you have mentioned as having been present during this order are not mentioned at the bottom of page 1 of this document. Are those names in addition to these names that are at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just note for the assistance perhaps of the witness that the footnote in the B/C/S version is on the first page and the second page, so if the Court usher could perhaps pass to the second page, the witness would know better who Your Honour is referring to. At least I think that's the case. There is a footnote on the second page, I'm not sure if it's a continuation or a part of the same -- or a part of a new footnote. Your Honour, we are doing our best to do everything through e-court because we understand that to be the preference of the Trial Chamber. I do have a hard copy in B/C/S. Given the flipping of pages, I'd be happy to provide it to the witness. I think it would make it easier for him, if that's an appropriate procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After the witness has seen it, if it could be passed on to the Defence counsel to have a look at it. Maybe if there is a hard copy of the English version that has any more names than what we are able to see in page one of the English version, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think that the English version you have is the English version that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall the presence of Milan Babic. Pavkovic, the Minister of the Interior, I do know that President Martic was there, as well as the close associates of the commander of the Main Staff, but I cannot recall whether the late Milan Babic, Pavkovic, and Prijic were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the footnote on page 1, Mr. Milan Babic is mentioned and indeed, yes, Mr. Milan Martic is also mentioned, so also General Celeketic, and then Mr. N. Pavkovic and Mr. I. Prijic, yourself, Mr. Raseta.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prijic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Prijic, okay, and Mr. Knezevic. But certainly, Mr. Loncar and some other member, some other person you mentioned earlier are not mentioned there. But all I want to know is whether those who are not mentioned there, whom you mentioned, were also present? Were they just omitted when this document was written or what the position is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible they were left out, but quite honestly I don't remember that Milan Babic, Pavkovic, and Prijic were there. As for the others, and as for the contents of the remainder of the report, yes, I know that that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you do remember that Mr. Milan Martic was there when the order was issued? And he left the office after that? That's what you testified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'm certain of that. This footnote is not contained in the document I had. I have my own document in front of me. This footnote was added by the chief of the intelligence department. I just extracted certain passages I needed in order to check certain information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Black. I'm sorry for interrupting your leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No problem at all, Your Honour. Thank you very much for the clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, one further point of clarification, several members of the Supreme Defence Council are mentioned by you and also in this footnote. Was this a meeting of the full Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. To the best of my recollection, it was a meeting of the collegium, General Celeketic with his immediate associates. We were in the office and President Martic came in when General Celeketic issued his order. I'm really confused by what it says here referring to Babic, Pavkovic and Prijic. I don't remember ever sitting in a meeting together with them, but I may be wrong. I'm not sure. I'm just not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. What was your own reaction when you heard General Celeketic give this order to shell Sisak?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Neither I nor any of those present reacted to the commander's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you surprised by the order in any way?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, because later it turned out that Gacic did not carry out this order because the targets had not been pinpointed precisely. He knew that were he to open artillery fire on Sisak there would be a lot of innocent victims which is why he did not open fire. Celeketic was angry. I don't think anyone of those present opposed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Milan Martic had any reaction to this order?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. None of those present had any reaction to Celeketic's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Whiting has helpfully pointed out to me, just as a matter of information that Sisak appears on page 21 of the atlas, Exhibit 23, and it's in grid C-3 if it's helpful to Your Honours in putting a context and location to what's being discussed right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Grid number C-3?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As Commander-in-Chief, Mr. Milan Martic had the power to countermand that order by Mr. Celeketic, did he.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all my questions for this document. It's already admitted into evidence so there is no need to go through that procedure right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, you referred to the meeting that was referred to in this document on the 1st of May 1995 was not a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council. Did you attend a meeting of the regular Supreme Defence Council in the early days of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember on which date that meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I think it was on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who was present at that meeting, to the best of your recollection? Just tell us what you can remember.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This was the meeting after the fall of Western Slavonia. Is that the one you're referring to? I'm not sure which one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. That meeting of the Supreme Defence Council, I think you said it was on the 1st of May 1995. That's the one I mean.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: You mean the extended meeting where the members, the ministers were, the members of the cabinet? Is that the one you mean? After Operation Flash? Is that the meeting you're referring to? There was more than one meeting so I don't know which one to focus on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let's focus on that one for the time being. Tell us who was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's the witness's problem. He's not quite sure what meeting. Maybe if you're able to indicate what was being discussed in that meeting or the agenda of the meeting, he might be able to focus on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I can focus it this way. It was a meeting where the members of the Supreme Defence Council -- it was a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council and other politicians were present. Do you have in mind the meeting that I mean? You just referred to it just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You referred to an extended meeting with cabinet members.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's the meeting referred to, the Supreme Defence Council, in an expanded composition, the ministers were there of the government, General Celeketic with his assistants, all of them, General Loncar, General Bjelanovic, Colonel Alavanja, Colonel Raseta, Colonel Knezevic, and President Martic who chaired the meeting. The purpose of the meeting was to analyse and explain the fall of Western Slavonia. At this meeting, which was opened by President Martic, Lieutenant Colonel Knezevic was first given the floor, and he spoke about the axes along which the Croatian forces had gone into action. After that, General Celeketic took the floor and spoke about how the Croat forces were supported by the 18 -- how the resistance was supported by the 18th Corps and that Western Slavonia should not have fallen. After Celeketic's speech, a decision had to be made as to how to proceed further. There were several ministers, I can't remember all their names, who proposed that there was no point in engaging in any further military operations and have soldiers and civilians get killed as a result, but that work had to be coordinated with the FRY and President Milosevic and that a solution had to be found to solve this situation by political measures and return the population that had fled from Western Slavonia to their homes. That's how the meeting ended. It ended on that note. Celeketic did not say anything, nor did President Martic, to the effect that weapons should be used to restore this territory. That's how the meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say that Celeketic did not say anything, nor did President Martic, to the effect that weapons should be used, was there any mention made of the possibility of an attack on Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Not at that meeting, no. There was no mention of any operations against Zagreb or any other town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was there any mention of the Orkan multiple-barrel rocket launchers at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't remember anyone mentioning it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
