utterances.text: Were you generally aware of the use and location of the Orkan rocket launchers during 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I never saw those artillery pieces but I knew of their existence, and I knew that they were physically guarded by my squad in the military police battalion, but I did not know of the precise location of that artillery piece. The first time when I took up my duties, I asked General Celeketic what my duties were with regard to the counterintelligence protection of that artillery piece, as it was the most important artillery piece in the possession of the army. He said to me, "That artillery piece is in a safe place and you have no obligations concerning it." After that, I no longer inquired about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know to whom the Orkan rocket launchers were subordinated?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff. I don't exclude the chief of artillery at the Main Staff, that he also knew where it was located. And the servicing of this multiple-barrel rocket launcher but I'm sure Celeketic knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so it's 100 per cent clear, I think you stated this already many times, but Celeketic was the Commander of the Main Staff. That's who you're referring to, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The -- yes, the Commander of the Main Staff, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to show you another document, with the assistance of the Court officer and the usher I'd like to show trial Exhibit 92, please. Colonel, please have a look at the document that's on the screen in front of you and just tell me what this document is. If you need us to scroll down so you can see the rest of the document, please just say so.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the Main Staff concerning the raising of combat readiness to the command of the 7th and 21st Corps and the military police battalion and it refers to the Orkan, that it should be ready for use on orders from Celeketic. All the preparations had to be carried out so that when the order was issued, it could be fired. It says in this document that there should be a march along certain axes, I don't know whether you need me to read this, that the Vojnic area should be reached at about 1400 hours on the 1st of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much. If we could just scroll quickly to the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It is Celeketic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is this document consistent with what you just told us about the subordination of the Orkans to General Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you of the that's all for that particular document. Again, this is already a trial exhibit, Your Honours. It's Exhibit 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to ask him to look at another document which will take more certainly more than three minutes. I'm wondering if it might be convenient to take the break now and start with the document after the break. But I'm happy to do it however you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We appreciate you letting us off early today more than once. Court will take a short adjournment. We'll adjourn and come back at quarter to six. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The next document which I'd like to show to the witness is trial Exhibit 95. With the assistance of the court officer and the usher, if we could bring that on to the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, if you could please just have a look at this document and tell me whether or not you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This is a security document which was created after the fall of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What's the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The document is dated the 2nd of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance again of the usher, if we could look at the last page, please. If we could scroll down to the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, does your name appear at the end of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you in fact draft this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How did you do so? How did you compile this document? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The better part of its contents I took over from a staff document and a part of it dealing with security-related issues was produced by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now I'd ask you to please look at the top of page 2. In fact page 3 in the English version. And when that appears on your screen, Colonel, if you could just tell me what is reported there. I don't need to you read it out but just tell me generally what's addressed.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It says here that on that day, at 10.30, certain targets were fired upon in Zagreb from eight Orkan rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Does it indicate any particular locations that were hit?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. The Ministry of Defence, at Krizaniceva street, the Zrinjevac area where the American embassy was partially damaged. Then the crossroads at the railway station and the Esplanade hotel, the building at Radnicka street as well as parts of Novi Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: There is also a reference to people killed and wounded. What numbers does it give for persons killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. About 30 killed and 130 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you have any information to indicate whether there were civilians among these casualties, among those killed and injured?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I think that they were -- they were civilians for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that something that you learned at the time or only later? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This became general knowledge later on, that it was civilians who were casualties of the rocket attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On that same day, the 2nd of May, did you receive any other information besides what was in this document, any other specific information about the shelling?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: There was discussion. I don't know who set that, that there were 30 people killed but I don't know who it was who talked about it. This sort of information could only be provided by security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know whether Milan Martic was informed about the consequences of the shelling of Zagreb on the 2nd of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't know about that. At any rate, the commander of the Main Staff had to report on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: To whom did he have to report on that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just -- it was just a clarification, you said, at any rate, the commander of the Main Staff had to report on that and I just wanted you to make clear who he had to report to about that.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: To the president of the republic, Milan Martic. He was also duty-bound to inform the General Staff of the FRY, based on that standing order issued by the General Staff, which we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you yourself learned of the shelling of Zagreb on the 2nd of May, what was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: My reactions were then and are still now that the persons who were familiar with these artillery pieces knew that they were intended for targeting wider areas and not points, and that as such they could entail a lot of casualties. I did not support such a decision and I stand by that view today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd now ask you to look at the last page of the document in B/C/S. This passage actually appears on pages 5 and 6 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Pages 5 and 6 in the English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, it's the part that is bracketed there that begins, "All those who participated in the discussion." That's the part I'm focusing on now. Did you draft this part of the report or is this something that you copied from someone else's work?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I wrote this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you please explain what you meant when you say that there were different approaches on how to resolve the situation? And then you talk about the position of Martic and Celeketic as opposed to others.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone, except for -- and I'm referring to the meeting where the Supreme Defence Council had an extended meeting with the presence of members of the cabinet, all of those present, except for Martic and Celeketic were in favour of a peaceful solution of the newly arisen situation through negotiations, as I've already explained, with a view to signing a cease-fire agreement binding on both sides, which meant that the population would return to the areas they originally came from. However, Martic and Celeketic were opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What was the preferred solution of Martic and Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I think that it was Celeketic who suggested that the territories lost be recaptured by combat, where the forces of the adjacent cause would be engaged as support. I know for a fact, however, that the commanders of the other corps which were supposed to take part in such an action were not in favour of the action and the territories lost were not recaptured because objectively speaking the 18th corps no longer had the strength necessary to recapture the territory. This was therefore Celeketic's proposal which was accepted by Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when you mentioned recapturing territory, which territory do you mean? Which territory would be recaptured?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I'm referring to Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Another question just for clarity, is this the same Supreme Defence Council meeting or the extended meeting that you talked about a little bit earlier in your testimony? Are you referring to the same meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I can't recall at present time whether this was that meeting or whether it was the meeting that followed this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's fine. If you can't recall, I think we can move along, unless Your Honour has a question.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the contents are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just have one question. You say there were two approaches, the one by Mr. Milan Martic and Mr. Celeketic to go on combat, and the other one by the rest of the members to negotiate a peaceful settlement. In the end, which of these two approaches prevailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The action referred to recapture the territories was not in fact carried out; however, what followed was the decision to open fire on Sisak, Zagreb, and some other towns. I don't know if I made myself clear. What followed was not a combat action aimed at recapturing these territories, in view of the fact that the commands of the Banija and Kordun corps were supposed to carry the action out together with the 18th Corps. Since this did not take place, a decision was taken to shell Zagreb and some other towns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In retaliation, not in defence n retaliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Those are all my questions with regard to that particular document. If we could turn now to trial Exhibit 100, please? And if we could just look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina, namely the commission for establishing the responsibility for the military organisation and the fall of Western Slavonia, which was signed by the commander of the Main Staff of the RSK, Colonel Celeketic. In other words, a commission was set up which investigated -- made an inquiry into all the circumstances surrounding the fall of Western Slavonia, the commission then produced a report and submitted it to the Main Staff of the RSK. The document is dated the 13th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Just one clarification, I think there may have been a mistake. The transcript reads, that this was signed by the commander of the Main Staff of the RSK. Was it signed by Celeketic or was it submitted to Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It was delivered to him. That's what the -- he's the addressee but, of course, I would have to look at the end of the document to see about the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps we could look briefly at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. The members of the commission signed the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, were you aware of this document in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I was aware of it in so far as my official, Colonel Nikola Suput was involved in the commission. However, there were no significant omissions on the part of those in charge of the security situation surrounding the fall of Western Slavonia, but I would have to read the document to refresh my memory further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's a fairly long document and I won't ask to you look at all of it. I'd like to direct your attention to pages 10 and 11. It's page 16 in English. And in particular, conclusion number 9. Colonel if you could just read that first line and then we'll pass over to the next page. I think we can pass to the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, it says there that no opinions were sought from the commanding officers of the SVK Main Staff. Is that consistent with your own recollection of events at this time?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As far as you know, were members of the SVK Main Staff consulted about the decision to shell Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I was focused on the text. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of course, that's quite all right. As far as you know, were members of the SVK Main Staff consulted about the decision to shell Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May 1995? And I mean members other than General Celeketic, of course.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The last sentence of this paragraph says the decisions were made by the commander and the president and stances and orders were given on the telephone. There are no written orders. Is that consistent with your understanding of how things happened?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Orders may be issued over the phone and in writing. However, if an order is put down on paper, although, of course, there was time for that as well, in that case, a wider circle of people would have been familiar with the order. What one can conclude on the basis of this is that commander Celeketic tried to transfer the -- over the phone in order to make sure that only he and the person receiving the order on the other end of the phone were the ones familiar with the order. What I wanted to say, of course, is that issuing orders over the phone is not something that is in dispute. However, the decision should have been collectively taken. We should all have been familiar with the order. In this case, this went through the closest associates of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. That's all I have to ask you about that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could now see trial Exhibit 101, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, please take just a moment to look at this and then tell us what this document is, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This is a document drafted by General Celeketic entitled, "Request for the removal of commander of the Serbian Army of Krajina." And it is addressed to the Commander-in-Chief, President of the RSK, Milan Martic. And the document is dated the 15th of May 1995. Probably, or rather certainly, feeling guilty for the fall of the -- of Western Slavonia, because prior to him assuming the position of the Commander of the Main Staff he was the commander of the 18th corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you see this document in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: General Celeketic did not show the document to his associates. He only told us what the substance of the document was, and it is as one can read it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So did he tell you personally that he was leaving the post of commander of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, if you would, please look at the second paragraph of this document. There, Celeketic writes, "I have acted in accordance with our doctrine of reprisal at the chosen vital targets of the combatant." Do you know what General Celeketic is referring to here?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He's talking about reprisals against selected vital targets of the opponent. However, I'm telling you this from my knowledge, from my military knowledge, based on the military schools I completed, this notion of reprisal is not something we encounter. What he is referring to here, under -- or by mentioning reprisals is the attacks that were launched against Zagreb, Sisak, and some other towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. That completes my questions on the issue of the shelling of Zagreb. I just have a few more topics to cover with you very, very briefly and then the Defence counsel will have a chance to ask his questions of you. First, were you present in Croatia at any time during 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. I wasn't until 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge or information about crimes that were committed in Croatian villages such as Saborsko or Skabrnja during 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No, I don't have any knowledge or information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When the RSK fell in August of 1995, where did you go? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Are you referring to me personally or to the service I was in charge of?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: To you personally.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Together with the Main Staff, we were relocated, first to Srb in Donji Lapac municipality, and after that, via Republika Srpska and Prijedor, we arrived in Banja Luka. So we were relocated in stages. This took several days. Then from Banja Luka, I returned to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and I think it was on the 14th of August 1995. I reported to my home unit, which had sent me to the war front.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In effect, did you then return to the service of -- to your prior service in the Yugoslav army, leaving the service of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. Because my post had been filled, and I could not be given an appropriate position, in view of my rank and the work I had done. I solved the remaining -- my financial problems I still had and other material issues, the writing of official evaluations and so on. This took a few months. And because I met the conditions on the 1st of January 1996, I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you retired -- I think earlier in your testimony you referred to the fact that service in the SVK resulted in certain benefits, including double time in terms of seniority or pension. Did you in fact receive double time for retirement purposes for the time you served in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like to show you one final document. It's a photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do that, can I just get clarity here? Mr. Raseta, you say that on the 14th of August 1995 you reported to your home unit which had sent you to the war front. When they accepted you there, as you returned, as what -- in what capacity did they receive you back? I'm asking the question because you say your position had been filled and you just had to finish off your reports. You were not -- in what capacity were you received back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the capacity of an officer not assigned to a particular duty. I was waiting to resolve all my administrative issues and then to retire. I filled in the application and it was accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The photograph which I'd like to show bears the ERN 04696912. In fact there are two photographs on the same page. If that could be put on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd simply like to ask you if you can recognise -- first, if you can recognise any of the people in these two photographs.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I recognise my former president, Milan Martic. I'm not sure but, yes, next to him is General Borislav Djukic in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you referring to the picture on the left or the picture on the right?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: On the left, the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And there are two gentlemen there in uniform -- well, actually there are two gentlemen in green camouflage uniform. Can you describe which one of those gentlemen you're referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: To the right of President Martic is General Borislav Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And then looking for a moment at the other photograph, are you able to tell us where that photograph was taken? Can you recognise the location?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think it's the fortress. I'm not sure, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The fortress in which city?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document containing the two photographs be admitted into evidence, please, and assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 458, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my co-counsel, Nikola Perovic, will conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Raseta?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you know I am one of the Defence counsel appearing for the accused. I am attorney at law, Nikola Perovic. I will now cross-examine you according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I would like to ask you one thing. As we speak the same language, let's avoid overlapping. Please make a pause after each question so that the interpreters can do their job. Thank you. From the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, I conclude that from the second half of October 1993, until the 14th of October 1995, that is for almost two years, you were first the chief of the analysis department and then the chief of the security organ with the Main Staff of the Serb Army of the Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 14th of August, not October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On page 6, in paragraph 14 of your statement, you say that while you were serving in the security organs of the SVK, the security organs did not register a single war crime or carry out an investigation of one. My question is the following: Were there such crimes or not?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't have any information about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you say, "I was in the region in the area during Operation Storm, August 1995 but I have no concrete knowledge of crimes committed by members of the HV, the Croatian army."

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No, I don't, because all communications with subordinate commands have been cut off. That was the only reason why we were unable to receive information, not just I but none of the subordinate organs could obtain relevant information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I see. In the next paragraph, under number 15, you say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I would just ask if we are going to continue to go through the statement if the witness could be provided a copy of it so that he can see what it was he actually included in the statement in order to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may extend the request, Mr. Perovic, you could also provide the Bench with copies of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any other copies apart from the one I'm holding in my hand. If the Prosecution has an extra copy, would they be kind enough to show it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Certainly. I think we have a copy in English and a copy in B/C/S and I think I can also provide another English copy, Your Honour, if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Won't you need your copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I have yet another marked-up copy for myself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Here is an English copy. And the translation for the witness. And I believe I have another set as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I thank my learned friends. Your Honours, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Perovic. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Raseta, on -- we are on page 6, and in paragraph 15 you speak of your contacts with Milan Martic. You say there were about 10 of these and that he asked you several times to use your security organs to prevent smuggling by SVK members, and you go on to say that Martic also wanted to achieve better cooperation between the civilian and military security services and that he told you that you could contact him whenever you felt the need to do so. How did you make use of this opportunity?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: You mean these ten contacts?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I mean the proposal Martic made to you.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: First of all, I haven't found this on page 6, in paragraph 15. That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's at the bottom of the page, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: During the time period?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Your question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: My question was, how did you make use of the opportunity created for you by Milan Martic when he asked you to use your security organs to prevent smuggling and crime?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I made use of it in the following way. The corps bordering with the 5th Muslim Corps, that was the Lika Corps, the Banija Corps, and the Kordun Corps, the security organs recruited their military police to take up check-points and to confiscate weapons and fuel that were being smuggled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asked to go into private session when he put a question to you in relation to something I'm going to ask you about now. I don't see any reason for it but out of an abundance of caution I now move that we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When responding to some questions put by the Prosecutor, you spoke about the relationship between the Serb Army of Krajina and the Army of Yugoslavia. What I'm interested in was the following. Did the Army of Yugoslavia, apart from the logistical support you described, provide any other kind of support for the Serb Army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. A group of officers arrived, three of them, who participated in drawing up the defence plans of the Republic of Serb Krajina, and also what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the period from 1992 to 1995, Mr. Raseta, five acts of aggression by Croatian forces on the territory of the RSK have been registered. Did the Army of Yugoslavia respond in any of those cases?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: You mean physically?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So not a single platoon or company or squad was sent to assist from the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No, not from among the active-duty soldiers, and I'm referring only to the period when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you know about this in general.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You've heard of the Vance Plan --

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: -- from January 1992. Are you aware that according to this plan, the Army of Yugoslavia was duty-bound, if UNPROFOR was unable to do so, to protect the Serbs in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't recall this but I don't have any reason to disbelieve you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 19, on page 7 of your statement, you say that although you did not receive an explicit order to inform him about events in the RSK or the SVK, you did this. I'm referring to Dimitrijevic, the chief of the security administration. Did you make this decision on your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It was something that not only I but all my predecessors did. They reported too. If need be, I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in paragraph 21, on page 8, you say the following: You say that your predecessors, whom you name, Vuk Dimitrijevic and Dusan Smijanic, did not systematically inform the head of the VJ security administration. In this respect, your activity would be exceptional; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the previous paragraph, paragraph 20, you say, "I did not tell Milan Martic, president of the RSK, and Lieutenant General Milan Celeketic, CGS SVK that I kept Dimitrijevic informed, Dimitrijevic being the chief of the security administration of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. I had the right not to inform them of this. To inform them of matters relating to my professional counterintelligence activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify something. Today, when answering a question put by the Prosecutor, you said that you did not tell Milan Martic about your sending information to the chief Dimitrijevic but that you did tell Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So which is correct, what you're saying now or what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I informed him from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 22, on the same page, you state that there was no formalised exchange of information between the SVK security organs and the security organs of the army of the Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 23, on page 9, you speak of the intelligence centre of the VJ at Petrova Gora, Kordun, which was used to collect information for the purposes and needs of the General Staff of the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence of this paragraph reads, "In my opinion, if the VJ really wanted to share its information and intelligence with the Serbian Army of Krajina, the main part of this intelligence centre would have been located at Knin and not at Petrova Gora."

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And can it be concluded on the basis of this that the Army of Yugoslavia and the Serbian Army of Krajina operated under the circumstances as a single tissue, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The information from the centre went directly to the General Staff, and it was precisely this Colonel Mihajlo Knezevic who was in charge of it in the part that had to do with the army of the RSK. Whatever was relevant for the RSK, Colonel Mihajlo Knezevic would receive the information as part of the security administration of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm interested in. Had the VJ General Staff really wanted to share the security information and intelligence with the SVK, your opinion was, as you put it, the intelligence centre would have been located at Knin and not at Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that the information was supposed to flow directly to us and then from us to Belgrade. This is something that should have been the case. For some reason, however, the information first went to Belgrade and was only then forwarded to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you just slow down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 24, on page 9, you speak of the exchanges of visits of some members of logistics support department, training, and operations department, and so on and so forth. And you say that the purpose of these visits was to draft plans of defensive -- for defensive operations of the SVK. My question is as follows: Were these plans always of defensive character? And I mean the plans that were drafted during such visits.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: During these visits, plans for the defence of the RSK were drafted. That was the purpose of the visits and I can tell you that for a fact, when it comes to these plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore these were defensive plans?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, for the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Raseta, on page 11, in paragraph 34, you mentioned that on one occasion, Martic told you that he could not consider all the Croats his enemies, and you repeated that today.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: During your -- today's testimony, why did you call into question his sincerity at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He was able to order Celeketic to fire upon Zagreb, and I don't know whether any other town was shelled too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore this was the sole reason that led you to doubt the sincerity of his words?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On page 12, in paragraph 35, you state that you were under the impression that Milosevic had firm control over Martic, and as an illustration of such influence wielded by Milosevic you mention the rejection of the Z-4 peace plan in early 1995. How would you explain Milosevic's negative reaction to the idea of unifying the two Krajinas, Croatian and Bosnian Krajinas, and his anger at the shelling of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I can explain this. I am merely relaying to you what I heard. And I have my opinion about it but what you're saying is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said, "I cannot explain this."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the Z-4 plan, you said that it was good for the Serbs and for Croatia today. This is what you state in your statement. Today, in response to the Prosecutor's questions, you stated that you were not that familiar with the plan. Then how could you comment today to the effect that it was good for the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: We talked about the plans -- the plan, and I mean the officers, as it offered a possibility to the Serbs to remain in their homes, to enjoy a certain degree of autonomy, and it opened the possibility for them to maintain cultural and other links with the mother country of Serbia and definitely had the plan been accepted, the Croatian action would not have followed and the Serbs would not have been driven away. At any rate, the plan offered the possibility for the Serbian population to remain in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And this is something you learned from these conversations by hearing these comments without you actually obtaining any further information about the plan?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, I was not able to, since I did not have the plan in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On page 14 of your statement, in paragraph 44, you state that you did not know the nature of the relationship between Martic and Jovica Stanisic but that you knew that Martic had to obey Stanisic, and you go on to say, "At the moment I'm providing you with this statement, I do not remember any concrete examples of this dominating position of Stanisic's vis-a-vis Martic." My question to you is: How did you arrive at the conclusion that Martic had to obey Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I know that when Stanisic was at Korenica, he was sent over there by Milosevic, a part of the Main Staff headquarters was at the forward command post at Korenica because we were supposed to carry out some plans vis-a-vis the 5th Corps of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Although I was not present at that meeting, there was Colonel Smiljanic, who was present there when Jovica Stanisic appeared on behalf of Milosevic, and transferred assignments to them. Among other things, General Celeketic said that he was not sure that -- whether he would be able to meet the requests put forth by Stanisic on behalf of Milosevic and then Stanisic said, well, if you can't do that, then someone else will. But he did ash and I mean Celeketic did not oppose Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And this was the sole basis for your conclusion that Martic had to obey Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, Stanisic went to the Pauk command at Petrova Gora more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This is something we will get back to later. Do you know, Mr. Raseta, what Milan Martic's attitude was towards Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that but I believe that they knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that Mr. Martic had asked that the -- he be removed from the territory of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I did not hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the relations between Milan Martic and Captain Dragan or Dragan Vasiljkovic were?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Based on my knowledge of Milan Martic and on my knowledge of Dragan Vasiljkovic, I believe that President Martic could not have a good opinion of Captain Dragan, but since the Serbian State Security sent him over there, he had to be tolerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything of the presence of the late Raznjatovic, aka Arkan on the territory of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 48, on page 15, you state your opinion that the state security of the Republic of Serbia had imposed Captain Dragan, Dragan Vasiljkovic on Milan Martic. Was this your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is this your opinion today?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, it is, because had we had the strength, we would have removed Dragan Vasiljkovic from the RSK. He had no business being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When discussing the relations between Milan Martic and Milan Babic, you mentioned the presidential elections in the RSK. You said that the elections were rigged in Milan Martic's favour. What is the source of your knowledge in connection with this?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: These were comments made publicly. It was discussed that Babic must have won the elections but that Milosevic could not come to terms with this and that the Republic of Serbia and the State Security there staged several events or, rather, carried out these clandestine actions which included the disposing of ballot boxes like the ones we found outside our command in order to declare the elections rigged and have new elections called and Martic elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, these, the knowledge you had, and I would say it was -- these were allegations, which boiled down to the comments, the stories, that went around Knin and the RSK. You have no other evidence in this respect?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. Except for the discarded ballot boxes we found.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I reminded you of this a moment ago and I have a question for you which has to do with this. On page 16, in paragraph 52, you state that in the summer of 1994, Radovan Karadzic was in Knin where he talked to the RSK leadership about the ways in which the RSK and the RS might come closer on the political and military -- political, government, and military levels, in view of possible future unification. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Smiljanic, whom you mentioned a moment ago, told you, in connection with this, that the big boss in Belgrade, did he refer to Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was not happy with this initiative at all. Is that the case? Was this in fact the case?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because of your statement or position that Milosevic wielded great influence over Martic. But this is something that deviates from what you state.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, I don't see how it does deviate, since there was no unification. In fact, it seems that Milan Martic went along with this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On page 17, in paragraph 55, you state that in 1994, there were two forward command posts, the abbreviation being IKM, in order to coordinate operations with the army of the Republika Srpska and with a view to providing support to the Cazin and Cazinska Krajina and Fikret Abdic. Do you wish to say that the RSK army formed the forward command post and that the VJ security administration formed such a post at Kordun, at Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This parallel command post at Petrova Gora in Kordun was known as the Pauk command; is that correct? And in paragraph 57 you go on to say that according to my information, Martic and Celeketic opposed the existence of a parallel command post at Petrova Gora. My question to you is: Why?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Why they were opposed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: They were opposed to that because it was impossible for two command posts to coordinate one action. You had to have one command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, Martic and Celeketic thought that this parallel post was being imposed on them?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And they were opposed to that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, they were opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On page 22, paragraph 71, you said that you had no information on the possible involvement of the Army of Yugoslavia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in general or Perisic as the chief of the General Staff of the VJ and Slobodan Milosevic in particular in the decision to shell Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May 1995. In the same paragraph, you state that from -- that you heard from Mihajlo Knezevic that General Momcilo Perisic ordered a VJ air force regiment stationed at Batajnica near Belgrade to raise its alert status and prepare airplanes for strikes against the Croatian forces outside the knowledge of Slobodan Milosevic. This was August 1995, and Operation Storm. You go on to say that when Milosevic found that out, the order was annulled, and no aircraft left Batajnica. You learned that from Mihajlo Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How much longer do you intend to go, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that I can complete my examination in ten minutes. If you believe this to be appropriate, in order for us not to resume the examination tomorrow, I can complete my examination in some 10 to 12 minutes. Of course, if the Prosecution agrees with that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know why I'm standing up but since I am standing up, I can say, Your Honour, that the next witness actually is not going to start testifying until Thursday. So I don't think there is any reason to sit over the 7.00 time today. I think we can finish this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it doesn't terribly inconvenience you because in any case there is still re-examination of the witness and questions by the Bench, Mr. Perovic. But I don't mind if you just want to round off a point and then you can carry on tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are no problems, Your Honour. I can complete my cross-examination of witness Raseta tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would this be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. The Court will adjourn to tomorrow at quarter past 2 in the same court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
